fits_channel: social; web; email; chat; marketplace; pr; sales-deck
wrong_when: the seller is a company and the promise needs the company behind it. tôi puts one named person behind a guarantee a team has to honour
why_it_matters: The one form the source lets out of the pairing rule: every other pronoun takes a matching form for the other side, and tôi takes any of them. It also carries equal status regardless of age, so it is the correct first person when the buyer's age is unknown - which online it always is

pairs_with: anh; chị; anh/chị; ông; bà; bạn; các bạn; quý khách; quý vị; các anh chị em; khách hàng
fits_channel: social; web; email; chat; marketplace; pr; sales-deck
wrong_when: the shop is one person. A sole trader writing chúng tôi is inflating, and buyers in small categories read it correctly as a template
why_it_matters: Documented exclusive: it means us and not you. This is the correct first person for a seller, and the reason chúng ta is not

wrong_when: the sentence means us the sellers. Then the word is chúng tôi, and chúng ta has quietly put the buyer inside the company
why_it_matters: Documented inclusive: it means you and me. Machine translation cannot see the difference because English we is both, so an English draft saying "we deliver in one day" comes back as chúng ta and now the customer is delivering. This is a grammatical error, not a tone preference
probe: Chúng ta cùng giữ cái nồi đó chín năm.

ambiguous_with: mình is the reflexive pronoun in all three persons and also the noun for body, so của mình can mean your own and biết mình is not first person at all
wrong_when: the buyer is a stranger and the category is one where deference is expected. The source restricts singular mình to intimate relationships, spouses among them
why_it_matters: On a one-person shop's page mình is warm and accurate. On a registered company's page it is a costume, and it clashes with every elevated form in the same piece
probe: Mình rang cà phê ở Gò Vấp.

wrong_when: the copy also carries a warranty, a licence number or a refund rule. The register and the obligation do not match
why_it_matters: Intimate and inclusive at once. It is the default voice of a small Vietnamese seller on social, and it is the correct choice far more often than chúng tôi is - provided nothing else in the piece is ceremonial

ambiguous_with: cháu is also the kinship noun for grandchild, niece and nephew, so it appears in copy that is describing a family rather than addressing anyone
wrong_when: the writer is not plainly younger than the reader. Claimed deference that the ages do not support reads as sales patter
why_it_matters: The documented reciprocal when the reader is addressed as ông or bà. A piece that says ông and then tôi is not wrong; one that says ông and then mình is

ambiguous_with: nước ta and quê ta mean our country and are ordinary modern usage; chúng ta and người ta both contain the string
wrong_when: always, in commercial copy
why_it_matters: The source gives singular ta as soliloquy or as a high official marking his own rank. In a product caption it arrives from machine-translated period drama, and it is the loudest possible signal that nobody read the draft

wrong_when: always, unless the piece is quoting somebody
why_it_matters: Superior to subordinate and familiar. The source calls the forms in this class impolite outside family use, and kinship terms are what replaces them

pairs_with: bạn; các bạn; anh; chị; anh/chị; mọi người
ambiguous_with: every proper noun in the draft, which is why this row carries no regex
wrong_when: the brand name is long, or the piece is a formal notice. Repeating a four-syllable name where a pronoun belongs reads as a press release
why_it_matters: Using the speaker's own name instead of a pronoun is documented practice, and the source names musicians, actors and models as the people who prefer it. For a personal brand it dissolves the register problem entirely: a name has no age and no tier. Advisory row - no detector can tell a brand name from any other proper noun

pairs_with: tôi; mình; chúng tôi; chúng ta; bọn mình; tên thương hiệu
ambiguous_with: bạn bè, bạn hàng and bạn thân are nouns meaning friend or partner, not address
wrong_when: the buyer is plainly older than the writer, or the category expects deference - property, healthcare, insurance, funeral services. The source records bạn as a recognised usage for readers in their early twenties, not as a neutral you
why_it_matters: There is no neutral second person in Vietnamese, and bạn is what machine translation reaches for because English you has no age in it. That single substitution is the most common register tell in translated Vietnamese copy

pairs_with: tôi; mình; chúng tôi; chúng ta; bọn mình; tên thương hiệu
wrong_when: the piece is a one-to-one message. An email addressed to các bạn was written to a list and did not hide it
why_it_matters: các is the documented pluraliser for address forms. Switching between bạn and các bạn inside one piece is the only legitimate switch in this table, because it is a change of number and not a change of tier

pairs_with: tôi; chúng tôi; em; tên thương hiệu
ambiguous_with: anh ấy and anh ta are third person; anh em means siblings; anh is also first person when a man addresses his partner
fits_channel: social; web; chat; email; marketplace; sales-deck
wrong_when: the reader's gender is not known. Then the form is anh/chị, and guessing is worse than the extra slash
why_it_matters: One of the small set the source allows in formal contexts, with tôi as the reciprocal. It is age-marked, which is the point: it says the writer has placed the reader, and placing them wrongly is worse than bạn

pairs_with: tôi; chúng tôi; em; tên thương hiệu
ambiguous_with: chị ấy and chị ta are third person; chị em means sisters or women collectively
fits_channel: social; web; chat; email; marketplace; sales-deck
wrong_when: the reader's gender is not known, same as anh
why_it_matters: The female counterpart in the formal set. A piece that addresses anh in one section and chị in another is fine when the sections are aimed at different buyers, and broken when they are the same section
probe: Chị đặt trước giúp em nhé.

fits_channel: social; web; chat; email; marketplace; sales-deck; pr
wrong_when: the channel is a short caption. Four syllables of politeness in a nine-word line is the whole line
why_it_matters: The workable default for a stranger of unknown gender, and what the source names as the modern replacement for the obsolete ngươi. Slightly formal, never wrong, and the address most Vietnamese SME sites and pages actually use - which is why it fits every channel except a caption with no room
probe: Anh/chị để lại số điện thoại.

ambiguous_with: ông ấy and ông ta are third person; ông nội, ông ngoại and ông chủ are kinship or job nouns
wrong_when: the reader is middle-aged rather than old and the channel is informal. The source allows the formal middle-aged sense, but on social it ages the reader
why_it_matters: The correct form for an elderly male reader, with cháu or tôi as the reciprocal. Categories that sell to older buyers get this wrong in the direction of bạn, which is not merely casual but incorrect
probe: Ông giữ hoá đơn này nhé.

ambiguous_with: bà ấy and bà ta are third person; bà nội, bà ngoại and bà chủ are kinship or job nouns
wrong_when: the reader is middle-aged rather than old and the channel is informal, same as ông
why_it_matters: The female counterpart. Paired with ông it covers an older audience without guessing an age band

ambiguous_with: em is first person when the seller defers to an older buyer and second person when the buyer is younger, and it is also a romantic endearment and the ordinary word for a younger sibling
wrong_when: used as second person to a buyer whose age is unknown. Calling a stranger em assigns them a lower rank, and getting that wrong is the one register error buyers reply to
why_it_matters: The dominant first person in Vietnamese retail chat - em gửi anh - and the reason a detector cannot simply count second-person forms. Which side of the conversation em is on depends on who else is named in the sentence
probe: Em gửi anh ảnh sản phẩm.

wrong_when: the seller is a small shop on social. This is the register of an airline and a bank, and on a home bakery's page it reads as a pasted template
why_it_matters: Documented as audience-elevating and still in current use. It is the safest form when nothing about the reader is known, and it costs warmth in exactly the channels where warmth is what converts
probe: Quý khách vui lòng giữ hoá đơn.

wrong_when: the piece sells anything. quý vị addresses an assembled audience, so in a product description it implies a room that is not there
why_it_matters: Also documented as audience-elevating, one tier above quý khách: esteemed guests rather than valued customer. Correct at a launch, a press statement or a stage script, and ceremonial anywhere else

wrong_when: the audience is a marketplace listing or an inbox. It addresses a gathering
why_it_matters: The documented way to address a mixed audience of roughly the writer's own age, with các ông bà anh chị em covering all ages at once. It is a greeting, not a copy-wide address form: a piece that opens on it and then settles into bạn has changed who it is talking to
probe: Kính chào các anh chị em.

pairs_with: tôi; mình; bọn mình; chúng ta
wrong_when: the piece is one-to-one, or the seller is formal elsewhere in the same piece
why_it_matters: Not a pronoun in the reference grammar - it is the noun phrase everybody - and it functions as one in current social copy. Graded as craft because the source does not attest it, not because it is rare
probe: Mọi người đặt trước giúp mình nha.

ambiguous_with: khách hàng is an ordinary noun, so it appears in copy that describes customers rather than addressing them, and both uses are grammatical
wrong_when: a real second-person form appears in the same piece. Then half the copy talks to the reader and half talks about them, and the reader can feel the seam
why_it_matters: The source allows virtually any person-noun to serve as a pronoun, so addressing the reader as khách hàng is not an error. What makes it a tell is the mixture, and the mixture is what a template produces: policy sections written about customers pasted next to body copy written to one
probe: Khách hàng nhận hàng trong 2 ngày.

wrong_when: always, in commercial copy
why_it_matters: The source lists it as obsolete and names bạn or anh/chị as what modern Vietnamese uses instead. It survives in machine translation of Chinese period fiction and in game localisation, and it is a different string from người, so a spellcheck will not find it

ambiguous_with: lông mày means eyebrow, which puts this string in ordinary cosmetics copy
wrong_when: always, unless the piece is quoting somebody
why_it_matters: Superior to inferior and familiar. Impolite outside family use, and the cosmetics collision is real: a brow product's description contains the string and means nothing by it

wrong_when: it carries a claim. người ta nói attributes a statement to nobody, and a claim with no holder is the one thing a competitor can report
why_it_matters: The widest-reference pronoun in the language - the source glosses it as they, people in general, generic one, we, someone - which is exactly why it is the Vietnamese studies show. If the claim needs a source, name it. If it does not, drop the attribution and state the fact
probe: Người ta nói cái này tốt.
